stories.headline: Democrats take the House and Senate, and Texas elects Gina Hinojosa governor and James Talarico to the Senate
stories.why_read: The story your whole timeline was about last night: a wave election that ran straight through Austin, with Texas electing its first Democratic governor in more than 30 years.
body: X's election roundups report that Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterms, setting up a divided government for the rest of President Trump's term. In Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott to become the state's first Latina governor, and state Rep. James Talarico beat Attorney General Ken Paxton for the open U.S. Senate seat, the first Democratic Senate win in Texas since 1988. The summaries say Democrats also took lieutenant governor, attorney general and other statewide offices.

Beyond Texas, the roundups list Senate flips in Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, including Kansas's first Democratic senator since 1932, Deb Haaland as New Mexico's first Native American woman governor, and Xavier Becerra as governor of California. The roundups credit strong Latino, Black and younger turnout, with voters focused on education and household costs, and Talarico's 'We just took back Texas' post from a Whataburger became the image of the night. Counts were still being finalized as of this morning, so expect some margins and calls to keep moving.

stories.headline: Matthew Honnibal says the 'Astra edits Qwen's weights' result is not what the headline suggests
stories.why_read: Yesterday's lead story got its most-upvoted rebuttal: the Qwen math jump came from Python code and practice runs, not from a model just staring at raw weights.
body: Matthew Honnibal, the creator of spaCy, went through every experiment in MIT's 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' post and tabulated which ones actually read raw weights, which wrote weights, which used Python and which ran the network. His finding: the pure 'just by looking at the raw weights' setting, with raw floats in context and no tools, only appears in three experiments on networks of 17K to 172K weights. Every experiment on a real language model used Python, and the headline Qwen3.5-0.8B result, MATH-500 going from 7.9% to 48.1%, also got to run the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems.

He compares the write-up to a magician doing the same trick three different ways, so each version seems to rule out the obvious explanation. Honnibal still credits GPT-6 Astra with doing the work a human ML engineer would do, which models from a year or two ago couldn't. His point is that those results don't belong in the same claim as the raw-weight reading. The post hit nearly 1,000 points on Hacker News, more than the original paper.

stories.headline: Postman's desktop app quietly installed plugins into Codex and Claude Code
stories.why_read: The top story on Hacker News: an API client reaching into your coding agents without asking is exactly the trust-boundary failure every dev team should check for today.
body: A GitHub issue filed against Postman's desktop app, marked SEVERE, documents what happened on one Mac after opening Postman 12.33.4. The user found a user-wide Postman plugin for Codex, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin and a separately installed Postman CLI. Codex then started routing API work through Postman's skills and throwing recurring MCP authentication warnings. The reporter also says the installer tried to mark its own startup hook as trusted.

The reporter's argument is simple: opening an API client shouldn't make it the default workflow inside unrelated tools. The thread hit more than 1,300 points on Hacker News, and a separate 'Tell HN: Don't use Postman' post climbed alongside it. If your team runs coding agents, it's worth checking their plugin and hook directories for anything you didn't install.

stories.headline: Tesla starts fully driverless Robotaxi rides in Fort Worth
stories.why_read: Another Texas city goes unsupervised: Fort Worth is now Tesla's third-largest no-safety-driver market after Austin and Houston.
body: According to X's summary of rider posts, Tesla began unsupervised Robotaxi rides in Fort Worth on November 2, with no safety drivers on board starting at 6 a.m. The service area covers about 143 square miles around downtown and reaches suburbs like Saginaw and White Settlement.
That makes Fort Worth the seventh U.S. city for the service, alongside Austin, Houston, Dallas, Miami, Orlando and Tampa. Early riders posted smooth trips, though some raised safety concerns.

stories.headline: SemiAnalysis says SpaceX is on track to become the world's biggest AI cloud, with 13GW in 18 months
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the analysis behind the claim that SpaceX may soon own a big slice of the world's AI compute, as Musk argues power is now the real bottleneck.
body: SemiAnalysis published 'Elon Is Doing It Again: SpaceX Will Be The World's Biggest AI Cloud,' arguing SpaceX can bring 13 gigawatts of AI data center capacity online in about a year and a half. Michel de Guilhermier, in another post you bookmarked, put it more bluntly: SpaceX may own 16% of the world's AI compute by the end of 2027.

It lines up with Musk's recent argument on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast that chip production will outrun electricity generation, leaving chips sitting idle without power. He has also said superintelligence compute will eventually move to orbit, but the ground buildout is the part happening now. X's summary of the debate notes turbines are already sold out.

stories.headline: On Linux, Nvidia's RTX Spark laptop runs inference at about a fifth of its Windows speed
stories.why_read: If you were eyeing an RTX Spark laptop as a local LLM box running Linux, read this first: an encrypted power table caps the GPU at around 780 MHz.
body: MindStudio dual-booted Linux on an MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop and found most things work, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia's open kernel driver, 4K at 120Hz, audio and the touchpad. The catch shows up on wall power. The GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux, versus about 2.2 GHz on Windows, and throughput on a 120-billion-parameter model drops from around 65 tokens per second to about 14.

The root cause is a Windows-only component, Nvidia's Platform Controllers and Framework, which manages power sharing between CPU and GPU. Its firmware power table is encrypted, so Linux can't read it. For now the write-up says WSL is the better route on this hardware.

stories.headline: OpenAI built Pando, a new Git backend for a monorepo flooded with Codex pushes
stories.why_read: A real look at what AI coding agents do to infrastructure: OpenAI says Pando cut median push latency by nearly 80% and now serves nearly a petabyte of Git data a day.
body: In 'Scaling Git at OpenAI,' the company explains that Codex drove so much concurrent work in its monorepo that it had to rebuild source control without changing how anyone uses Git. Pando stores each pushed packfile as an immutable blob and records branch tips in a horizontally scalable metadata store. Unrelated branches update independently, pushes to the same ref stay serialized, and fetches reuse cached packs instead of building a fresh pack for every client.

Per The New Stack, Pando was written in Rust in 10 weeks, with one engineer designing the core and teams of Codex agents implementing it, and it went into production in April. OpenAI also describes a Git conformance suite and deterministic simulation testing to catch race conditions. If your repos are starting to feel agent traffic, this is the first big public account of where Git breaks.

stories.headline: DeepSeek reportedly plans to pre-train V5 mainly on Huawei Ascend chips
stories.why_read: If it works, it's the first frontier-scale open model trained mostly without Nvidia, a real test of whether export controls can hold.
body: According to reports summarized on X, DeepSeek will pre-train its next major model, DeepSeek V5, mainly on Huawei's Ascend 950 chips, starting as early as late 2026 and ramping in 2027. DeepSeek has so far used Ascend mostly for inference. The plan reportedly involves Huawei engineers working closely with the lab and a data center in Inner Mongolia planned for 160,000 chips.

The move is driven by U.S. export limits on Nvidia hardware. Earlier attempts to train on domestic chips had mixed results, and performance gaps remain. If V5 ships with open weights and competitive scores, it will be the strongest evidence yet that China can train frontier models on its own silicon.

stories.headline: Simon Willison got Qwen 3.8 27B on his laptop to interpret model weights too
stories.why_read: The fun counterpoint to the Astra debate: a model you can run locally manages one of the paper's weight-reading tricks.
body: Simon Willison took one of the examples from MIT's 'Sparks of Weight-Space Programming' post, where a model is handed a text dump of a small network's floating-point weights and asked what it does. He ran it against Qwen 3.8 27B on his own laptop and reports that it could interpret the weights as well.

It's a small experiment, not a replication of the full paper, but it suggests the raw-weight reading part isn't limited to frontier models. Read it next to Honnibal's critique for the full picture of what was and wasn't shown.

stories.headline: Developers say OpenAI quietly switched model training back on for their Codex chats
stories.why_read: If your company opted out of training on Codex, check the setting today: several engineers found it re-enabled without opting back in.
body: A Hacker News post that reached about 490 points says a team that had carefully disabled data sharing across Codex, Claude Code and similar tools found the 'Improve the model for everyone' setting turned back on in Codex. None of them had knowingly opted back in. The poster linked an earlier thread reporting the same thing.

The setting lives in ChatGPT's data controls, and commenters pointed to OpenAI's privacy portal as a second place to opt out. There's no official explanation in the thread. A separate post the same day says Gemini personal subscribers can't opt out of training without turning off chat history.

stories.headline: Paying Gemini subscribers can't stop chat training without giving up chat history
stories.why_read: A good reminder that a paid personal plan doesn't mean your chats stay out of training; Google's own help pages say so.
body: A Tell HN post quotes Google's Gemini help pages: with Keep Activity on, saved Gemini chats are used to improve Google services, including training generative AI models. A subset of chats is read by human reviewers, and reviewed chats are kept for up to three years even if you delete your activity.

The only way out is turning off Keep Activity, which means chats disappear after 72 hours. Google warns users not to enter confidential information. For work data, the takeaway is to use enterprise accounts with contractual terms rather than personal subscriptions.

stories.headline: GitBook says an attacker using AI agents got into its infrastructure credentials
stories.why_read: If your docs sync through GitBook, rotate your Git Sync secrets and API tokens; the company's own notice says they may have been accessed.
body: A customer posted GitBook's support reply to Hacker News. It says GitBook was hit by 'a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents' starting at 19:00 CET on November 2, when the attacker got some infrastructure credentials. GitBook took the app and authenticated docs offline, replaced every credential and secret, and invalidated every customer's API tokens.

The notice says the attacker may have accessed Git Sync secrets, GitBook API tokens, third-party API tokens and questions visitors asked GitBook Assistant, with no evidence so far that content was modified. The poster said they hadn't seen a public breach notification yet.

stories.headline: GitHub had a morning outage hitting pull requests, Git operations, Issues and Actions
stories.why_read: If your pushes or CI failed early this morning, this was why; GitHub marked it resolved at 5:50 a.m. Central.
body: GitHub's status page reported elevated errors and intermittent failures across Pull Requests, Git Operations, Issues and API requests this morning. Updates posted between 11:17 and 11:30 UTC said the API, Git and PR degradation had been mitigated, and Actions was mitigated at 11:43 UTC.
The incident was marked resolved at 11:50 UTC (5:50 a.m. Central), with a root cause analysis promised later. Worth a glance if you saw odd CI failures before work.

stories.headline: IEEE Spectrum: PHP2Shell shows AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
stories.why_read: A clear explainer of the PHP bug that put WordPress and Drupal sites at risk, and why AI bug-hunting will keep surfacing old code like it.
body: Dina Genkina writes that PHP2Shell was the biggest of a run of late-October security disclosures. It put sites like NASA's, Wikipedia and the White House, plus everything else running WordPress or Drupal, at risk of exploits that could read data and run code on the server. Researchers reported it to the PHP Foundation and a patch shipped before attackers had the exploit.

'All the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,' Tolmo's Matt Suiche told Spectrum. 'Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.' The piece argues AI tools make old memory bugs much cheaper to find, for defenders and attackers alike.

stories.headline: Fujifilm is quintupling magnetic tape production because AI is generating so much data
stories.why_read: A nice reminder that the AI boom runs on boring infrastructure too: LTO tape is having its biggest moment in decades.
body: Ars Technica reports Fujifilm will invest about 10 billion yen (roughly $63 million) to raise its tape capacity fivefold compared with fiscal 2025 levels. The money goes to its Odawara site in Kanagawa from fiscal 2026 through 2028, mostly to make LTO Ultrium10 tape. Fujifilm calls it its largest investment yet in dedicated LTO facilities.

The company points to 'exponential growth' in data needs driven by generative AI. Tape stays attractive for cloud-scale backup because it's cheap per terabyte and sits offline, which protects it from ransomware.

stories.headline: Stringman is an $795 open-source robot that hangs a gripper from your ceiling corners
stories.why_read: A clever answer to robot cost: four motors and four cables reach an entire room, including floors too cluttered for wheels or legs.
body: Neufangled Robotics' Stringman suspends a gripper from lines anchored in the four ceiling corners. Because all four motors share the load, it lifts up to 2.2 kg near the floor and about 1.9 kg on average across a 7 by 7 by 3 meter room. The company compares that to about 0.32 kg for a typical seven-actuator arm using the same motors. It moves at about 0.4 meters per second and uses two anchor cameras.
It's open source and can run air-gapped, which helps it stand out from cloud-tethered home robots. It reached about 640 points on Hacker News.

stories.headline: The Vesuvius Challenge reads writing in another Herculaneum scroll for the first time in 2,000 years
stories.why_read: Machine learning plus CT scans keep pulling text out of scrolls carbonized in AD 79, and PHerc. 306B just joined the list.
body: PHerc. 306 was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, excavated in the 1750s and micro-CT scanned last year, but nobody had read it. After reviewing 25 community submissions, the Vesuvius Challenge awarded a $50,000 First Letters Prize to Liam Warner and Nicola Bodill for revealing ink and recovering readable text from PHerc. 306B.

The ink also settled which half of the broken scroll is which: 306B is the upper part, which makes the smaller 306A piece even more worth scanning and virtually unrolling. It's one of the best ongoing examples of open collaboration and AI tools doing real science.

stories.headline: The largest study of its kind finds young-onset colorectal cancer looks different at the cellular level
stories.why_read: Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer death for Americans under 50, and this Nature Medicine paper starts to explain why it's more aggressive in younger patients.
body: Researchers from Dana-Farber, Mass General Brigham and the Broad Institute report age-related differences in tumor makeup and gene activity in colorectal cancer, published in Nature Medicine. They describe it as the largest study of its kind and a foundation for understanding why the disease can be more aggressive in younger adults.

U.S. diagnosis rates for people under 50 rose 2.9% a year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society, and younger patients are more often diagnosed at advanced stages. Worth sharing with anyone who's been putting off a screening.

stories.headline: Geoffrey Hinton says humanity might have been better off never developing AI
stories.why_read: The Nobel laureate whose research underpins neural networks warns of a possible large-scale incident, like a temporary financial or power blackout, as soon as this year or next.
body: In a Guardian interview, Hinton, 78, said he is not a 'doomer' and that AI could lead to a 'wonderful future,' but that 'it might be that we would have been better off never developing it.' He warned that a large-scale incident, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems, could happen this year or next.

He said that within a decade, and possibly sooner, we'll know whether humanity can manage the risks and reach what he calls 'radical abundance,' or ends up with a huge gap between rich and poor and mass unemployment.

stories.headline: SpaceX unveils Starfall, a reusable capsule for drug research in microgravity
stories.why_read: SpaceX is turning orbital manufacturing into a product: weeks of microgravity, Starlink on board, and a parachute ride home.
body: Per X's summary, Starfall is a 10-foot-wide reusable capsule that rides on Falcon 9 and offers up to 1,000 kg of payload, 1 kW of power, Starlink connectivity and weeks in microgravity. It returns by parachute to the Pacific.
The pitch builds on work like space-grown crystals of the cancer drug Keytruda. Commercial customers have signed on, including Redwire, whose pharmaceutical labs are slated for 2028 missions.

stories.headline: Menlo Ventures: enterprise AI spending hit about $177 billion this year, up 5.4x
stories.why_read: Useful numbers for any architecture conversation: agents now drive most token usage, and coding tools are the biggest app category.
body: Menlo Ventures' annual report, as summarized on X, puts 2026 enterprise AI spending at $176.8 billion, up from $33 billion in 2025. It says autonomous agents now generate 80% of tokens on platforms like OpenRouter, and frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI captured 86% of LLM API spend.
Anthropic's share of API spend reportedly rose to 55% while Google's fell to 9%. Coding tools led applications at $34 billion out of a $77 billion app market.

stories.headline: Anthropic's S-1 shows $33 billion in nine-month revenue and a $104 billion net loss
stories.why_read: The IPO filing numbers are out, and Polymarket odds on the listing dropped as traders digested the losses and compute commitments.
body: According to X's summary, Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 and a $104 billion net loss, mostly from non-cash adjustments on convertible notes. Revenue growth slowed to 47% in Q3 as compute costs rose, and the filing lists $895 billion in long-term infrastructure commitments.

Polymarket odds on the IPO dropped on the news, though the summary also highlights Anthropic's 15-person chip team using Claude to speed custom silicon design ahead of a listing expected later this month. Charlie Bilello, in a post you bookmarked, had Anthropic's Q3 revenue up 1,127% year over year, so the growth story and the loss story are both real.

stories.headline: Critics say Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars on losing candidates
stories.why_read: One of the night's most-shared threads in your timeline: Musk's political spending, and his own joke that his 'election-interfering space lasers' didn't work.
body: Ron Filipkowski posted that Musk 'just incinerated $475 million backing losers,' and another post you reposted called it a bad night for Musk, who it said 'wasted half a billion' and now faces a Congress hostile to him. These are critics' figures, not audited totals.

Musk replied with a joke about his 'election-interfering space lasers' not working, according to X's roundup. The cd_hooks post you reposted added that he'll now face a hostile Congress and a Texas state government that 'loathes him,' which is worth watching for SpaceX and Tesla, both based in Texas.

stories.headline: Tarrant County and Texas's 23rd District flip too
stories.why_read: The Texas wave went deep: the largest Republican-run county in the country and a border district that includes Uvalde both went Democratic.
body: County commissioner Alisa Simmons beat incumbent Tarrant County Judge Tim O'Hare with 57.7% of the vote. She'll be the first Democrat in the job since 1986 and the first Black woman to hold it. Per X's summary, O'Hare conceded, and Democrats also lead the commissioner races that could give them control of the full court.

In the 23rd Congressional District, stretching from San Antonio to El Paso, Katy Padilla Stout beat Republican Brandon Herrera, the gun maker and YouTuber known as The AK Guy, leading 52% to 44%. She becomes the district's first Latina representative, and Herrera conceded.

stories.headline: India's UPI now handles more transactions per day than Visa
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: a public, open payments rail out-processing the world's biggest card network is a systems story as much as a finance one.
body: Rishi Bagree's post puts UPI at about 822 million transactions a day versus Visa's 650 million, which would make India's Unified Payments Interface the world leader by daily volume. These are the post's figures, and they compare count, not dollar value.

UPI is run by the National Payments Corporation of India and lets any bank app or wallet send money instantly by phone number or QR code. It's become the model other countries study for open, interoperable real-time payments.

stories.headline: He jailbroke his Renault's navigation unit just to change the clock
stories.why_read: A classic hacker story, about 860 points on Hacker News: a car that refuses to let you set the time unless you have the navigation map SD card.
body: The author drives a 2014 Renault Latitude. When Estonia switched from summer to winter time, he found the 'Set time' option missing from the head unit's menus. The previous owner had warned him the car needed its navigation map SD card just to change the clock, and that card had long since been thrown away.
What follows is a patient reverse-engineering of the head unit to get the clock option back. It's a great read about how much everyday hardware hides behind arbitrary software gates.

stories.headline: Why Namespace racks hundreds of MacBook Pros in a data center
stories.why_read: Coding agents need Macs to build iOS apps, and Apple left few options; this is the engineering behind a viral unboxing video.
body: Namespace's Kirill Nikolaev explains the company's custom Mac racks, built from hundreds of MacBook Pros. Its customers build and test iOS apps, which requires a Mac, the iOS Simulator only runs on macOS, and App Store releases need a recent Xcode.

The post covers how they start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and ship new Xcode versions hours after Apple releases them. It's a good look at what CI for agent-written mobile code really takes.

stories.headline: There's no posttraining data commons, and that's a problem for open models
stories.why_read: A sharp explainer on why open LLMs could fall behind: pretraining had the web, but agentic posttraining needs tasks nobody has published.
body: Open Athena's David Hall notes that pretraining got lucky. Wikipedia, open-source code, Stack Exchange, arXiv, Project Gutenberg and Common Crawl's roughly 10 petabytes made a ready-made commons. GPT-3 was about 60% Common Crawl-derived data, and open models like Nemotron still rely on it.

Posttraining, especially for agents, is different: 'Pretraining consumes documents, while posttraining consumes tasks.' Those tasks, with environments and feedback, aren't lying around in public. Hall argues that without a shared commons for them, truly open frontier models will struggle to keep up.

stories.headline: Mikko Hypponen: future programmers will look at the Linux kernel like we look at the pyramids
stories.why_read: A one-liner for the AI coding era that's funny because it might be true.
body: Security researcher Mikko Hypponen posted that future programmers will look at the Linux kernel the way we look at the pyramids of Egypt, wondering 'How the hell did they build like that with the tools they had?'
It lands on a day when Hacker News is full of AI writing code, AI finding old bugs and arguments about who still knows how to program.

stories.headline: Remembering Jeremy Brett, the Sherlock Holmes of Sunday Doordarshan
stories.why_read: A warm one from your feed: Jeremy Brett was born on November 3, 1933, and for a generation in India his Holmes was a Sunday ritual.
body: You reposted a tribute to Jeremy Brett (3 November 1933 to 12 September 1995) on what would have been his 93rd birthday. Brett played Holmes in Granada Television's long-running series, and many still consider his the definitive version.

Yansan's thread, which you bookmarked, remembers the mid-80s, when Doordarshan was almost the only TV window in India and 'The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes' aired every Sunday for thousands of fans. A small, kind corner of a very loud news night.
